title: Waterborne Diseases and Public Health: Risks and Interventions
authors: Dunga K.E.
abstract: Waterborne diseases remain a pressing global health issue, accounting for approximately 485,000 deaths annually from diarrheal illnesses and affecting over 2 billion people who lack access to safe drinking water. These figures highlight the critical relationship between water quality, sanitation, and public health outcomes, especially in low-resource settings. This chapter focuses on identifying long-term, sustainable interventions for preventing and managing waterborne diseases through a multifaceted, integrated public health approach. The findings emphasize that effective disease control requires combining infrastructure development with household-level water treatment, improved sanitation, and widespread hygiene education. Advanced surveillance techniques, including the use of Geographic Information Systems, play a vital role in mapping high-risk areas and informing targeted interventions. Moreover, the chapter explores how environmental changes, seasonal variability, and the rise of antibiotic-resistant pathogens complicate waterborne disease dynamics, necessitating adaptive strategies. It stresses the importance of international collaboration, policy alignment, and stakeholder engagement in supporting resilient water systems. Community-centered initiatives, culturally informed health campaigns, and ongoing monitoring contribute to long-term success. The chapter also presents case studies that demonstrate the effectiveness of integrated approaches, particularly when backed by robust governance and cross-sectoral cooperation. Therefore, safeguarding public health from waterborne diseases demands a comprehensive framework that bridges infrastructure, behavior change, innovation, and policy. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Water Safety in Sub-Saharan Africa
authors: Izah S.C.; Jacob D.E.; Alum E.U.; Fayiah M.
abstract: Water safety is a critical public health and development challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa, where millions lack reliable access to safe drinking water. This chapter examines the status, determinants, and impacts of water safety in the region, focusing on the quality and availability of water sources, contamination risks, and the associated burden of waterborne diseases. Drawing on empirical studies and regional data, it highlights key threats including microbial pathogens, chemical pollutants, inadequate infrastructure, climate variability, urbanization, and displacement. Case studies from countries such as Rwanda, Ghana, Nigeria, and the Horn of Africa illustrate both progress and persistent barriers to water safety. The chapter reviews relevant policy frameworks, such as the WHO Water Safety Plans and regional commitments to Sustainable Development Goal 6, and evaluates community-based and technological interventions aimed at improving water quality. Institutional capacity gaps, fragmented governance, and limited data systems are identified as core obstacles to sustained improvement. The chapter concludes with actionable recommendations focused on strengthening water governance, scaling up investment in infrastructure and hygiene education, and promoting multisectoral collaboration for sustainable, equitable water access. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Focal Box 3: Water. Flows of Power and Networks of Solidarity
authors: Hamza N.H.T.
abstract: Water is a central resource in Sudan for the production and reproduction of both the rural (pastoralists and farmers) and urban populations. Despite the importance of the waters of the Nile, since early times, due to the constraints imposed by aridity, seasonality, and a lack of infrastructure, Sudanese communities have had to rely on varied and complex socio-technical systems supported by traditional knowledge and principles of water-sharing in order to guarantee that their needs will be satisfied. British colonisation was a milestone in the country’s waterscape: first, it designed a new role for the State, which became a major actor in the regulation and modernisation of water resources, prioritising economic productivity through the construction of dams-beginning with the Sennar Dam on the Blue Nile (1925) and the Jezira Scheme for cotton cash crops, the largest in the world. Second, it fostered a new “moral economy” of expert bureaucracies that upset livelihoods, legitimised displacement, and undermined the autonomy of local communities regarding access to water and its use. The first post-colonial governments pursued policies that favoured huge infrastructures, regardless of the increasing awareness of their ecological and social costs, and they were maintained alongside a lack of attention to problems with the domestic water supply, which were mitigated in rural or peri-urban settings by the communities’ hold on small-scale water systems (wells, ?afir reservoirs, karro water carts) and water solidarity networks. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Climate extremes in agriculture: Managing drought and flood challenges
authors: Kesharwani S.; Singh A.
abstract: The intensifying climate variability amplifies the coupled drought and flood risks, exposing the limits of fragmented, infrastructure-only water strategies. This work aims to develop a drought-first, flood-aware framework that stabilizes water supply, reduces disaster losses, and strengthens equitable livelihoods across rural and urban settings, and to translate episodic flood surpluses into dependable reserves for dry periods while safeguarding ecological flows and public health. The chapter synthesizes case evidence, established hydrologic tools, runoff estimation, reservoir routing, channel capacity analysis, operational rule curves, hedging strategies, and nature-based measures. It evaluates strategic floodwater utilization (check dams, infiltration basins, managed aquifer recharge), multipurpose reservoir operations, and decentralized energy-water systems (micro-hydro with water-lifting) under explicit maintenance and governance scenarios. Integrated measures increased drought reliability by improving groundwater banking, irrigation efficiency, and demand management, while reducing flood damages through floodplain restoration, adaptive releases, and safe conveyance. Performance gains were contingent on routine operation and maintenance, locally anchored technical capacity, transparent allocation rules, and inclusive community engagement. Equity screening improved benefits targeting and reduced disproportionate impacts on vulnerable groups during deficits and inundation. A coordinated program centered on conservation, reuse, recharge, and dependable upkeep converts hydrologic variability into managed supply, narrowing the gap between scarcity and excess. Such integration provides a practical pathway to durable water security, safeguarding production and ecosystems under increasingly volatile hydroclimates. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Smart Water Infrastructure
authors: Kumar C.S.; Manasa N.; Bhargavi G.; Pal A.
abstract: Smart water infrastructure (SWI) is an innovative answer to the universal water issues- population growth, urbanization, industrial demands cross, and climate change exacerbating such challenges. SWI embraces advanced technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and cloud computing that allow more dynamic and responsive systems instead of the traditional systems that suffer unrecoverable losses, excessive energy, and degraded quality. It is already possible to reconfigure service delivery, minimize waste, optimize energy use, and achieve greater reliability than was used to be the case. The four main elements of SWI, which are IoT sensors, predictive analytics, automated controls, and central data storage, make early warning of leaks, demand, and supply management, and strategic management of certain resources possible. Since it seeks to solve fundamental problems such as non-revenue water and exposure to contamination, SWI is in support of the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically, the clean water and sanitation goal stated in SDG 6 and the sustainable cities and climate action goals, SDG 11 and 13, respectively. Some of these successful implementations include the IoT solutions for water in Singapore, smart irrigation in India, or urban water networks in Barcelona, to name a few. All these examples promise a better reach, quality, and sustainability of services. However, there are limits in regional and global scale applications of SWI practices, such as high upfront costs, legacy systems, technological divide, or even concerns of data leakage. To tackle these, novel financial, governance, and human capital development approaches need to be implemented. Thanks to advancements in technology as well as the development of equitable strategies, SWI embodies the rationalization of water use in the present environment, which will be asymmetric in terms of environmental and social benefits for generations to come. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Soufiane Haddout and Tonni Agustiono Kurniawan; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: The Intelligent Drop: Challenges and Ethical Implementation of Smart Water Technologies in the Pursuit of SDG 6 and Global Water Security
authors: Dhaya R.; Renugadevi R.; Kanthavel R.; Ranjith Kumar P.
abstract: Access to clean and safe water remains a persistent global challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. While Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) calls for universal and equitable access to water and sanitation by 2030, achieving this target requires leveraging innovative, scalable, and intelligent technologies. Smart water systems, powered by Internet of Things (IoT) devices, artificial intelligence (AI), and real-time monitoring have the potential to revolutionize water management by optimizing distribution, detecting leakages, monitoring quality, and enhancing governance. However, the rapid deployment of these technologies raises critical ethical concerns related to data privacy, social equity, environmental impact, and governance accountability. This chapter provides a thorough examination of smart water technologies from an ethical and sustainable development perspective. It addresses critical technical, infrastructural, and policy issues and presents a four-principle ethical framework based on fairness, autonomy, nonmaleficence, and transparency. Real-world case studies from Singapore, India, South Africa, Israel, and the United States are examined to demonstrate the potential and drawbacks of smart water initiatives. The chapter concludes with actionable recommendations and outlines future research directions that center on participatory design, decentralized models, and culturally responsive innovation. This chapter provides a roadmap for developing inclusive, resilient, and responsible smart water solutions that match with SDG 6's goal by combining ethical foresight and digital innovation. © 2026 A. Jose Anand and Saravanan Krishnan.

title: REVISITING: Off-grid, the New Water Supply Solution
authors: Gaudry A.; Colon M.; Baron C.
abstract: Drawing on recent research, policy reports, and interviews, this chapter explores what the term "off-grid" – originally borrowed from the energy sector – means in the water sector. Off-grid water solutions encompass a wide range of arrangements, many of which have long existed to serve populations whose needs are unmet by water utilities. What has changed over the past decade, however, is the shift in perspective: once viewed as temporary fixes until network expansion, off-grid solutions are now increasingly seen as a desirable and sustainable option for achieving SDG 6.1 (universal access to safe and affordable drinking water). This chapter critically examines the expectations placed on off-grid solutions and reviews the challenges that must be overcome to position them as a viable alternative to centralised piped water supply. A key question emerges: How should public authorities adapt the governance and regulation of complex, fragmented water supply systems in order to ensure equity, continuity, quality, and protection of water resources? © 2026 selection and editorial matter, François Molle and Sylvain Barone.

title: Water Governance and Sustainable Development Goal 6: Strategies and Insights from Central Himalaya, Nepal
authors: Pant R.R.; Gautam S.K.; Basnet N.; Awasthi M.P.; Joshi K.R.; Bishwakarma K.
abstract: Nepal, with its diverse topography spanning the Tarai Hills and the Himalayas faces unique challenges in water governance. The federal structure of Nepal, comprising 7 provinces and 753 local levels, plays a crucial role in implementing strategies for sustainable water management and achieving Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) targets. Water resources in Nepal stimulate the economy, supporting agriculture, hydropower, and fostering sustainability. This study focuses on the status, progress, and challenges in providing access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene in alignment with SDG 6 in Nepal. Despite notable advancements, with 95.47% of households in 2021 having sanitation facilities, only 56.97% relied on tap/piped water. Challenges include inadequate water supply systems, climate-induced disasters, and coordination gaps among the three tiers of the Government. Enhancing governance mechanisms and aligning initiatives with SDG 6 are crucial strategies for achieving both national and global targets and involve focusing on stakeholder collaboration to ensure equitable water and sanitation access, as outlined in the Constitution of Nepal 2015 (Articles 30, 35) and in governance structures (Schedules 5–9). Implementing national water policies, establishing regulatory bodies, and promoting community-driven management are essential steps. Additionally, addressing institutional fragmentation and fostering hydro-diplomatic relations with neighbouring countries are vital. Enhanced financial support and capacity-building efforts are also necessary. By prioritizing sustainable water management, Nepal can achieve its SDG 6 goals by 2030. © The Royal Society of Chemistry 2026.

title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence in Wastewater Monitoring and Treatment
authors: Fan Z.; Liu X.
abstract: With increasingly stringent requirements for medical waste discharge and growing water quality fluctuations, traditional monitoring and treatment methods based on manual experience and preset control logic exhibit significant shortcomings in real-time perception, process regulation, and timely equipment fault monitoring, making it difficult to achieve refined, low-cost collaborative operation. In this respect, this paper develops a smart monitoring and treatment system of medical wastewater with a profound incorporation of artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. Using a multi-source sensor network, continuous measurements of the indicators that are relevant like COD and ammonia nitrogen are realized. The aeration rate, chemical dosage, and sludge return ratio are optimized dynamically using ANN-GA algorithm and a 24-hour water quality trend prediction is performed with the use of LSTM/Transformer models. Simultaneously, CNN-LSTM model is presented to forecast the remaining equipment life and preventive maintenance decisions to achieve a closed-loop control of prediction-control-maintenance. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed model has less COD prediction RMSE of 9.75, high proportion prediction R2 of 0.957, and early warning improvement in the water quality prediction F1 of 0.93 than the traditional methods. The rate of effluent compliance improved to 99.2% as well, unit energy consumption reduced to 0.63 kWh/m3, and the chemical consumption rate per unit was lowered to 0.029 kg/m3. To the extent of operation and maintenance, the operation and maintenance had an extension of 4.6 days warning of equipment failure, unplanned downtime reduced to 2.1, and maintenance expenditure cut down to 27.3%. Studies have revealed that smart systems that are enabled by artificial intelligence have the potential to enhance the reliability, cost-effectiveness, and safety of medical wastewater treatment systems, which is a technical route through which medical facilities can obtain accuracy and sustainable functioning.  © 2026 The Authors.

title: Education and Behavioral Changes for Safe Water Usage
authors: Jacob D.E.
abstract: Access to safe water is fundamental to public health, yet millions remain exposed to waterborne diseases due to unsafe water usage and sanitation practices. This chapter examines how education and behavioral change can serve as transformative tools in promoting safe water use at individual, household, and community levels. It explores the role of formal curricula, community-based campaigns, digital platforms, and emergency education in reshaping habits and fostering public awareness. The chapter applies behavioral theories such as the Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behavior, and Social Cognitive Theory to explain motivations and barriers influencing water practices. It also identifies key risk factors including socio-economic limitations, cultural beliefs, and gender roles. Case studies from global WASH programs highlight successful strategies like Participatory Hygiene and Sanitation Transformation (PHAST) and Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS). The chapter further addresses monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, outlining tools and indicators that assess progress. Finally, it presents institutional frameworks and policy recommendations for scaling and sustaining change. Through interdisciplinary integration of education, psychology, and community engagement, the chapter provides a holistic roadmap for fostering water-safe behavior. It concludes that without educational investment and sustained institutional support, infrastructure improvements alone cannot guarantee long-term water safety and public health outcomes. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Sustainable Consumption: The Role of Behavioral Change Strategies
authors: Tweneboah-Koduah E.Y.; Adams M.; Mann V.E.
abstract: Sustainable consumption is essential for achieving sustainable development, yet translating sustainability awareness into everyday consumer action remains a major challenge, particularly in developing countries. In Ghana, rising plastic waste, low recycling rates, sanitation pressures, and limited adoption of sustainable household practices illustrate the persistence of the sustainable consumption attitude–behavior gap. Although many consumers express concern for the environment and support sustainable lifestyles, their actual consumption decisions are often constrained by affordability, convenience, weak infrastructure, limited information, greenwashing, social norms, and low access to sustainable alternatives. This chapter examines how behavioral change strategies can help promote sustainable consumption in Ghana. It conceptualizes sustainable consumption as a multidimensional practice involving environmental protection, economic viability, and social well-being across the selection, use, and disposal of goods and services. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior, Social Cognitive Theory, Social Learning Theory, the Transtheoretical Model, and the SHIFT framework, the chapter explains how attitudes, perceived control, self-efficacy, habits, emotions, social influence, and contextual conditions shape sustainable consumption behavior. It further discusses behavioral strategies such as nudging, default options, incentives, social norms, priming, and community-based interventions. The chapter argues that awareness creation alone is insufficient; sustainable consumption must be made easier, affordable, visible, socially desirable, and institutionally supported. By situating behavioral change within Ghana’s sustainability challenges, the chapter contributes to debates on how context-specific behavioral insights, policy support, and institutional partnerships can advance responsible consumption and Sustainable Development Goal 12. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Remote Sensing and Artificial Intelligence Driving Liquid Intelligence for Water Sustainability Financing
authors: Irfan M.
abstract: Financing sustainable water andsanitation remains a criticalchallenge in achieving global development goals. Despite progress, billions still lack access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation due to funding gaps, weak governance, and rising climate pressures. This paper, Liquid Intelligence Financing Water Sustainability throughRemote Sensing andArtificialIntelligence, explores how innovative financing models, including blendedfinance, microcredit, andpublic–private partnerships, can be strengthenedthroughtechnologicalintegration. Remote sensing provides accurate data on water resources, quality, and scarcity, while artificial intelligence enables predictive analytics, smart infrastructure management, and optimized investment decisions. Together, these tools enhance transparency, efficiency, and resilience in financing frameworks. The study argues that combining financial innovation with data-driven intelligence not only advances SDG 6 but also fosters equity, health, and long-term economic sustainability. title: Cybersecurity of SCADA/ICS Used in Water Management: Threats, Incidents and a Practical Defence Blueprint
authors: Mishra A.
abstract: Water and wastewater utilities rely on SCADA/ICS to run treatment and distribution, but modernization has exposed them to credible process risk. Internet-reachable HMIs, weakly governed remote access, flat networks, legacy platforms and vendor pathways enable adversaries—from “hacktivist” brands to state groups using living-off-the-land (LOTL) tradecraft—to alter setpoints, suppress alarms or force manual operations. Incidents across two decades and multiple countries (e.g., Maroochy, Oldsmar, Aliquippa; adjacent “fluids” cases like Colonial and TRITON) show how small configuration mistakes and governance gaps scale into environmental, safety or service impacts. This chapter consolidates lessons learnt and prescribes a practical, measurable blueprint aligned to NIST SP 800-82 and ISA/IEC 62443: remove exposure; segment with an Industrial Demilitarized Zone (IDMZ); govern remote operations with MFA, jump hosts and PAM/JIT access; deploy process-aware monitoring for LOTL behaviours and anomalous plant states; and rehearse backup, rebuild and manual operations. Executed over 12 months with clear KPIs and ownership, these controls deliver defensible architecture, faster detection and resilient recovery. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Neha Sharma, Abhineet Anand, Abhishek Kumar, Rajeev Tiwari, Anupam Tiwari, and Prateek Thapar; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: Planning Challenges for Sustainable Cities in Bangladesh: A Radical Perspective
authors: Roy S.; Sowgat T.
abstract: This chapter offers a critical examination of sustainable urban development in Bangladesh, focusing on the paradox between economic growth and persistent urban challenges. Cities like Dhaka have become engines of national development, yet they remain plagued by deep-rooted issues such as socio-spatial inequality, inadequate infrastructure, environmental degradation, and poor service delivery. The chapter identifies that these problems are intensified by neoliberal planning models that prioritise economic efficiency and market-based solutions over social equity and environmental sustainability. Weak institutional capacities further hinder effective urban governance, leading to disjointed planning efforts and poor coordination among agencies. Although national policies and sustainability strategies claim to promote inclusive urban development, they often fail in practice due to a lack of financial resources, implementation capacity, and alignment with local needs. This is particularly visible in the rapid loss of green spaces, inadequate housing, and deficient access to clean water and sanitation services. The chapter ultimately calls for a fundamental shift away from growth-centric, externally driven development models. It advocates for equity-centred urban policies that are context-sensitive, locally informed, and designed to promote long-term sustainability and social justice in Bangladesh’s urban future. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Water for the Future or a Future for Water? SDG 6, Smart Water Technologies, and Sustainable Use
authors: Bello-Bravo J.
abstract: While smart water technologies offer promising tools for advancing the global water security indicators of Sustainable Development Goal 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), ethical discussions in this area rightly focus on access, privacy, and governance. However, a more fundamental question is often overlooked: Is the water being ethically delivered and monitored ultimately used for more sustainable purposes? Unlike other resources, water is often not consumed through use; instead, it is displaced, degraded, or sequestered, making it a paradoxical candidate for sustainability. This chapter argues that smart water ethics must include upstream evaluation of water’s end uses. It examines how ordinal ranking scales can help assess which uses of water are more or less sustainable over generational timescales, thereby informing policy- and decision-making about those uses. Framing water as a long-term investment, the chapter proposes that returns from smart water applications (particularly in municipal and industrial contexts) can be treated as "savings" and then allocated to water-insecure regions through infrastructure, social, and environmental development. In this way, the surplus from otherwise exclusively industrial/municipal smart water applications can benefit the rural/agricultural sectors, especially in the Global South. © 2026 A. Jose Anand and Saravanan Krishnan.

title: Liquid Assets: Financing Clean Water and Sanitation for Sustainable Development
authors: Irfan M.; Arora P.
abstract: Access to safe and sustainable water and sanitation continues to be a significant global concern. Many regions still struggle to provide reliable services because of limited financial resources, institutional weaknesses, and growing climate pressures on water supplies. This paper examines how financing approaches, including blended finance, microcredit, and public–private partnerships, can be strengthened through the practical application of technology. Tools such as remote sensing improve understanding of water availability and quality, enabling more informed planning and allocation of resources. In addition, advanced data analysis supports better risk evaluation, operational efficiency, and long-term infrastructure management. The study concludes that when financial strategies are supported by accurate data and sound governance, they become more transparent, accountable, and capable of attracting sustainable investment. Such an integrated approach supports universal access to water and sanitation while promoting public health, social equity, and long-term economic resilience. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. All rights reserved.

title: Toward SDG 6 in the Deduru Oya Basin, Sri Lanka: Assessing Localized Progress in Rural and Urban Settings
authors: Gamage D.; Ranasinghe P.; Nagabhatla N.; Chandrasena N.; Jayasena C.
abstract: Water is essential for society, the environment, and the economy. Achieving the Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) targets is therefore critical for community, regional, and national development. The successful implementation of SDG 6 is underpinned by key pillars, including governance, finance, capacity development, and monitoring, which collectively form an effective operational framework. Good governance is a fundamental pillar of SDG 6. It comprises essential components such as policy formulation, legal framework development, strategic planning, coordination, funding, capacity building, data acquisition, monitoring, and regulation. This chapter highlighted the importance of water security as a key element of the sustainability agenda related to SDG 6. Localized challenges are often overlooked in national progress assessments for SDG 6, which can lead to ineffective development strategies. Access to water, as well as progress toward achieving the targets of SDG 6, differs across local contexts, even within the same watershed, due to various socioeconomic, climatic, environmental, and geographical factors. This chapter specifically focused on irrigation improvements and engineering innovations’ impact on enhancing water use efficiency within a quasi-cultural context. Therefore, this study assessed Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators 6.1– 6.4 in the Deduru Oya basin in Sri Lanka. This vulnerable basin has less than 20% of its population with access to safely managed drinking water and sustainable sanitation services. Nonpoint source pollution, caused by agricultural runoff and poor waste management, seriously threatens the region’s water sources, risking human health and ecosystem integrity. With their historical significance and adaptability to local conditions, Indigenous water management systems provide valuable insights for developing effective solutions. However, several challenges remain, including limited data availability and the complexities of integrating traditional practices with modern water management techniques. Moreover, significant issues regarding water use efficiency and sustainability are further exacerbated by climate change, which threatens the availability and quality of water resources. The “Use to Resource Ratio” indicates that over 40% of the basin’s water resources are currently overexploited. The analysis showed that water-related challenges in Sri Lanka are often localized, highlighting the necessity to address the needs of marginalized communities that are frequently neglected in water resource planning. This study proposed tailored solutions to achieve SDG 6 by 2030, advocating for integrating indigenous knowledge with modern water management practices. The proposed solutions focus on establishing robust monitoring systems, enhancing capacity building, and fostering active community engagement to ensure equitable access to water resources and to bolster resilience against climate impacts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: Vital Role of Wastewater Treatment in Sustainable Development Goals for a Cleaner Future
authors: Rawat G.; Dewali S.; Miglani R.; Parveen N.; Siddiqui U.; Kumar A.; Bora S.; Arya M.; Sharma N.; Melkani D.C.; Dash S.P.; Bisht S.S.
abstract: Wastewater treatment protects public health and the environment, making it essential to sustainable development. This chapter explores the connection between wastewater treatment and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), highlighting the importance of effective wastewater management. The chapter explores the complex relationship between wastewater treatment and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), showing how successful treatment helps achieve varied SDGs. Untreated wastewater degrades the ecology and poses serious health risks. The chapter explores conventional and modern wastewater treatment methods and technologies, highlighting their usefulness in reaching Sustainable Development Goals. It also explains worldwide and national wastewater treatment rules and regulations, which set sustainable wastewater management requirements. The abstract proposes comprehensive cleaner future options in view of these problems and restrictions. These solutions include technology advances, regulatory reforms, capacity training, and public involvement to improve wastewater treatment efficiency and SDG alignment. The manuscript calls for a global effort to manage wastewater sustainably and emphasizes the need to act now to create a cleaner, more sustainable future. © Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: Sustainable rehabilitation of post-mining land through community-driven ecological practices in Bangka Belitung, Indonesia
authors: Herdiyanti H.; Suyanto B.; Mas'Udah S.
abstract: In Bangka Belitung, Indonesia, extensive tin mining has left thousands of mining pits (kolong), nutrient-poor sandy soils, and severely degraded ecosystems. This paper analyzes a community-driven rehabilitation initiative in Sinar Jaya Jelutung Village that seeks to restore abandoned mining land while securing sustainable livelihoods. Using a qualitative case study design, data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observation, and document analysis to examine ecological improvements and collective action's social drivers. Results show that villagers, organized through local farmer groups, manually cleared land, constructed simple bunds and drainage channels, and applied locally available organic amendments, particularly cattle manure supplied through a government livestock program, to rehabilitate roughly eight hectares of ex-tin-mining land. These gradual measures improved soil aggregation, stabilized water supply, and enabled continuous wet-rice cultivation, with recorded yields averaging 4.8 t ha-1 and peaking at 5.1 t ha-1. Equally significant, strong kinship ties, reciprocal labor arrangements, and trust-based networks mobilized labor and resources, while bridging and linking relationships facilitated access to external inputs and technical guidance. A hybrid governance arrangement, combining community initiative with enabling but non-directive state support, allowed local actors to adapt external resources to site-specific ecological conditions. Yet persistent challenges, including insecure land tenure, overlapping permits, and unstable market channels, reveal that technical soil improvements alone cannot guarantee long-term sustainability. The case demonstrates that successful post-mining restoration in tropical landscapes depends on the synergy of ecological techniques, social capital, and supportive policy frameworks, offering a transferable model for sustainable post-extractive development across Southeast Asia.  © Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd.

title: Advancing Water Quality and Safety in the Global South Through International Partnerships and Sustainable Development Goals
authors: Ogwu M.C.; Ulimboka R.; Izah S.C.
abstract: Ensuring equitable access to clean and safe water remains a critical global challenge, particularly in the Global South, where systemic inequalities, climate vulnerability, and infrastructural deficits converge. This chapter explores how international partnerships, under the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), notably SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), are advancing water quality and safety in low- and middle-income countries. It synthesizes interdisciplinary evidence from case studies, institutional frameworks, and policy mechanisms to evaluate how global cooperation facilitates technology transfer, capacity building, financial innovation, and knowledge sharing. Drawing on examples from East and Southern Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America, the chapter examines how public–private partnerships, South-South collaborations, and multilateral initiatives address water governance through inclusive and locally responsive approaches. It critically interrogates the risks of dependency, unequal power dynamics, and short-termism that often undermine impact, while highlighting successful strategies rooted in community engagement, gender and youth inclusion, digital innovation, and decentralized governance. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the necessity of aligning water partnerships with climate resilience, biodiversity protection, and justice-oriented transitions. In advancing both conceptual and practical insights, this chapter contributes to reimagining water partnerships as transformative instruments—capable not only of achieving SDG targets, but also of fostering enduring systems of solidarity and sustainability. The findings provide actionable guidance for scholars, policymakers, development practitioners, and communities striving to build inclusive, accountable, and future-ready models of water governance in the Global South. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Integrating Sustainability and Practice into Engineering Education: An Interdisciplinary Curriculum Model in Côte D’Ivoire
authors: Schmitt L.; Newiadomsky C.; Graßmann A.; Kouakou A.P.; Kre N.R.
abstract: This chapter presents a successful curriculum model that was implemented at a university in Côte d’Ivoire. The model emphasises sustainability and practical experience through an interdisciplinary dual-study engineering programme. It was developed under the project “Industry-Integrated Dual Engineering Study in a North–South Collaboration” (IIDES-NSC). The curriculum combines academic training with practical experience through demanding semester-long study projects and multiple industry internships, addressing the urgent need for energy and water supply solutions in rural Côte d’Ivoire by educating and training students to develop and implement new solutions. A central objective is to integrate sustainability not as a standalone subject but as a cross-cutting principle throughout the curriculum. This is exemplified by the development of a solar-powered prototype for electricity generation, water supply and water treatment. This approach directly supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly clean energy (SDG 7), clean water (SDG 6), quality education (SDG 4), gender equality (SDG 5), decent work and economic growth (SDG 8), and industry, innovation, and infrastructure (SDG 9). An interdisciplinary approach was central to the curriculum development. Stakeholders, including academic institutions, ministries, local industries, and international organisations such as German Society for International Cooperation (GIZ), collaborated through round tables, workshops, and surveys to align the curriculum with the industry’s needs and the country’s national development plan. The implementation faced challenges, including bureaucratic and cultural barriers, language differences, and a tight schedule. Acceptance of the curriculum’s practical orientation required the inclusion of industry-based lecturers and a focus on applied learning. Nevertheless, these challenges presented opportunities to enhance the university’s reputation, improve teaching quality, and better prepare graduates for the labour market. The chapter’s objective is to show how an industry-integrated, sustainability-focused curriculum can enhance employability, foster innovation, and strengthen higher education’s contribution to sustainable development. The curriculum demonstrates how a practice-oriented education model can empower students by addressing real-world challenges and leveraging collaborative development. The case study illustrates the transformative potential of embedding sustainability into curriculum design, offering a replicable model for similar contexts in sub-Saharan Africa. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Commercialization and industrial applications of waste-derived catalysts
authors: Kumar M.; Kumar S.; Gupta P.
abstract: Catalysts prepared from wastes (such as industrial wastewater, agricultural wastewater, or municipal wastewater) have recently been proposed as a new alternative to catalyze sustainable H2 production and other industrial processes in line with the circular economy principle. Sourced from fly ash, red mud, rice husk, and e-waste, this chemical-rich material acts as the catalyst to facilitate cost-effective water splitting, biogas reforming, and degradation of pollutants by reducing the dependence on costly virgin materials. They bring added value to industrial processes and may help reduce carbon footprints by adding value to waste streams rich in silica, alumina, and precious metals, like, for example, platinum and palladium. However, commercialization is limited: large differences in waste composition, regulation compliance, and market acceptance are hampered by reliability issues. Cost- and environment-effectiveness is demonstrated from favorable case studies of zeolite from fly ash and biochar catalysts from agricultural waste in petrochemicals and renewable fuels. Hybrid-nanostructured catalysts with the support of friendly policies like EPR can contribute to their potential. Concerning the problem of scale-up and standardization of the waste-derived catalysts, the technology would be able to contribute to the sustainable development of related industries, reduce environmental pollution, and promote the construction of a resource-conserving society. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Applying inclusive development as a strategy for sustainable development in South Sumatera Province
authors: Widiana D.A.; Ajrina F.I.; Antiqasari S.N.; Meraldha A.R.
abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of inclusive development as a strategy for sustainable development in South Sumatera Province. The research employs a qualitative approach based on a literature review using secondary data from planning documents, regulations, scientific articles, and official statistical reports. The findings indicate that, although South Sumatera has significant potential in the agricultural, energy, and mining sectors, several fundamental challenges hinder the achievement of inclusive development. Poverty remains at 12.27%, access to safe drinking water is only 53.54%, and only one out of approximately 2,800 villages has achieved self-sufficiency, reflecting significant regional disparities. Additional challenges include weak institutional coordination, limited funding, low participation of marginalized communities, and resistance from dominant actors. These findings align with the principles of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities). To strengthen inclusive development in South Sumatera, it is recommended to implement affirmative policies based on spatial data, enhance access to basic services, strengthen the socio-economic capacities of local communities, and promote participatory governance. The application of these strategies is expected to accelerate the achievement of SDG targets and foster more equitable, inclusive, and sustainable development.  © Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd.

title: The Future of Humanitarian Response in Crises: The Role of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Achieving Sustainability Through Advanced Technology
authors: Al-Makhzoumi O.; Al-Amro D.H.E.
abstract: This paper aims to highlight the important factors of the International Committee of the Red Cross, hereinafter referred to as ICRC, in humanitarian responses during crises and armed conflicts. It then centers on a discussion of modern technology aimed at sustaining ICRC’s humanitarian interventions. The institution is described to use modern technological innovations in its response to crises through improved logistical support, water and sanitation services, and monitoring compliance with international humanitarian law. The study discusses and identifies ways in which ICRC uses digital technologies in accessing essential humanitarian aid such as medicines and medical equipment through smart logistics platforms that ensure timely availability in conflict-affected areas. It emphasizes the importance of advanced technologies in ensuring good clean water access and sanitation projects through innovative solutions. In its monitoring efforts, ICRC uses modern communication technologies to track the enforcement of international humanitarian law in conflict zones and interactive platforms put ICRC ahead in education and awareness-raising on international legal frameworks. The organization further enhances its monitoring of detainee conditions with cutting-edge technologies, which advances the assurance that detainees will be treated per world humanitarian standards. This paper has been presented to highlight the incorporation of advanced technology into humanitarian response measures as a means of sustaining interventions by ICRC in crises to better humanitarian conditions and protect the rights real persons at stake in armed conflicts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Latin America’s Water Crisis: Pollution, Governance, and Community Responses
authors: Ogwu M.C.; Merritt H.; Martínez M.O.
abstract: Latin America’s water crisis is a multidimensional challenge shaped by environmental degradation, socio-political inequality, and institutional fragmentation. This chapter offers a comprehensive analysis of the causes, impacts, and responses to water pollution across the region. Rapid urbanization, industrial expansion, unsustainable agricultural practices, and inadequate wastewater treatment have severely compromised the quality of rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Climate change further exacerbates these challenges through intensified droughts, floods, and altered hydrological cycles, putting additional strain on already fragile water systems. The chapter highlights how weak regulatory enforcement, corruption, and uneven decentralization have created governance vacuums in which polluters often operate with impunity. Marginalized populations, particularly Indigenous and rural communities, bear the brunt of this crisis, facing disproportionate exposure to contaminated water sources and limited access to basic sanitation and healthcare. Drawing from case studies across Bolivia, Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil, the chapter explores the dynamic role of community-based organizations and grassroots movements in resisting water injustice and advancing alternative water governance models grounded in traditional ecological knowledge. Technological and policy innovations, including decentralized water treatment, nature-based solutions, transboundary cooperation, and participatory monitoring, are analyzed as potential strategies to build resilience and equity in water management. The chapter also identifies critical gaps in data infrastructure, indicator harmonization, and citizen science integration that hinder effective decision-making. By situating Latin America’s water crisis within a broader Global South perspective, this work contributes to interdisciplinary discourse on environmental justice, sustainable development, and the democratization of water governance, offering pathways toward more inclusive and accountable water futures. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Pathways to Resilience - Aligning Health, Climate, and Communities in the Asia-Pacific
authors: Wijesekara N.
abstract: Climate change is a defining health challenge for the Asia-Pacific, where geographic exposure, rapid urbanization, and entrenched social inequities combine to heighten risks. This chapter examines its health consequences through five interconnected pathways that capture the links between climate hazards, vulnerability, and capacity. Together, these pathways illustrate how climate change acts as a risk multiplier, compounding existing health burdens and creating cascading effects on communities, health systems, and economies. The analysis points out the importance of alignment across health systems, communities, and sectors beyond health. For extreme weather events, disaster risk governance must be linked to inclusive community-based approaches and supported by digital innovation and resilient infrastructure. Vector-borne disease risks call for strengthened surveillance that integrates formal and community-based systems, combined with One Health coordination across human, animal, and environmental health. Heat-related impacts can be reduced through multisectoral action that combines early-warning systems, public education, resilience-oriented architectural design, and renewable energy solutions. Water- and food-borne diseases require closer coordination between water utilities, health authorities, and communities, supported by tools such as Water Safety Plans, resilient wastewater management, and household water treatment practices. Food insecurity, intensified by climate change, demands investment in climate-smart agriculture, resilient supply chains, nutrition-sensitive programs, and regional cooperation through mechanisms such as grain reserves and early-warning systems. By discussing solutions across these pathways, the chapter highlights that technical interventions alone are insufficient. Building resilience requires participatory governance, equity-focused policies, and collaboration across sectors and borders. Only by aligning health systems, climate-responsive strategies, and empowered communities can the Asia-Pacific region transform vulnerability into resilience and secure a healthier, safer, and more sustainable future. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. title: Efforts and Disparities in Self-help Infrastructure Provisioning and Maintenance in Unplanned Neighborhoods of Zaria Urban Area, Nigeria
authors: Oladimeji J.S.
abstract: Most neighborhoods in cities of the Global South are largely characterized by unplanned or informal nature of physical development. This characteristic has led to the involvement of informal means of providing urban services and infrastructure in such places. This study examined the nature of local arrangements for infrastructure provision in four selected neighbourhoods of Zaria, a city in Northern Nigeria. The study adopted a largely qualitative approach of research, using observations, interviews and group discussions involving major stakeholders in each neighbourhood. The study findings revealed that each neighbourhood had their respective approach to infrastructure provision, as residents were found engaged in self-help initiatives like individual efforts, manual labour, household financial contributions, lobbying power, and the use of Community Development Associations (CDA), towards improving their environment and gaining access to basic urban services in the area of water supply, power, street and drainage improvement, solid waste collection and disposal. The outcomes of the individual neighbourhood efforts yielded varying levels of success and challenges. The study findings led to the conceptualization of the logic of neighbourhood collective influence in self-help initiatives, where the nascent, post-nascent and stabilized types of unplanned neighbourhoods were identified. This categorization showed that population size, population influence, and the capacity for organization determines the outcomes of collective self-help efforts in urban infrastructure services provisioning and maintenance. The study recommended among other things, that governance institutions should do more in assisting unplanned neighborhoods with technical and financial support as residents engage in self-help efforts towards improving their neighbourhood infrastructure and services. This will help make such self-help efforts to be easily upgraded into the formal city system of infrastructure. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: South and Southeast Asia’s Flooding and Water Contamination Crisis
authors: Ogwu M.C.; Jintrawet A.
abstract: South and Southeast Asia is facing a compounded environmental crisis at the intersection of climate-induced flooding and widespread water contamination, with profound implications for human health, ecological stability, and regional development. This chapter critically examines the systemic drivers and cascading consequences of recurrent flooding across diverse typologies, including flash floods, riverine inundation, urban waterlogging, and coastal surges, and their role in mobilizing biological, chemical, and emerging contaminants. Drawing from interdisciplinary evidence and region-specific case studies from Bangladesh, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam, the chapter demonstrates how infrastructural fragilities, governance failures, and socio-spatial inequalities exacerbate exposure to waterborne pathogens, heavy metals, and persistent pollutants such as arsenic and microplastics. The analysis foregrounds vulnerable populations, particularly those in informal settlements, who bear the brunt of both infrastructural neglect and institutional exclusion. By bridging insights from environmental science, urban planning, and public health, the chapter advances a holistic framework for resilience grounded in adaptive infrastructure, inclusive policy design, and regionally coordinated responses. It also underscores the strategic relevance of community-based knowledge systems, decentralized wastewater solutions, and digital innovations (e.g., geospatial flood mapping) in strengthening disaster preparedness and water security. In reframing Southeast Asia’s water crisis as a multidimensional governance and equity challenge, the chapter contributes novel pathways for research and policy integration in climate-vulnerable regions. The chapter repositions flooding and water contamination as interconnected governance and justice challenges—rather than isolated environmental events—providing a platform for rethinking integrated water management under climate uncertainty. It calls for an urgent, interdisciplinary reorientation of water and disaster management systems to avert a deepening cycle of socio-environmental risk. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Sanitation Management Strategy In East Lombok Using SSK Instruments
authors: Dwiyanti L.; Agustawijaya D.S.
abstract: Wastewater management and sanitation in East Lombok over the past 5 years received a portion of the APBD of 0.67% only. East Lombok in 2021, had the safe access to sanitation in 2.4% of the national target in 2024, that was 15%, so the gap is -12.6%, while the achievement of adequate access sanitation reached 75.8% of the national target of adequate sanitation in 2024, that was 90%, so the gap is - 14.2%. This research aims to analyze the sanitation needs of East Lombok and formulate sanitation management strategies to meet the 2026 sanitation targets. The methodology applied in this research is the SSK (District Sanitation Strategy) instrument method with gap analysis and SWOT analysis. From the results of research on infrastructure needs to increase access to domestic wastewater in East Lombok until 2026, that was the construction of 1301 units of septic tanks, 11,525 SR of residential wastewater treatment plants, 656 SR of residential wastewater development, 624 SR of urban wastewater treatment plants, 0.7 m3/day increase in IPLT services., and procurement of 1 unit of waste truck. Recommendations for strategies for handling sanitation in East Lombok are: Increasing access to safe sanitation from 2.7% to 7.6% in 2026, Providing a fleet for desludging & transporting fecal sludge, Revitalizing IPLT and establishing a domestic wastewater UPT institution, Providing regional regulations for domestic wastewater management, Increasing socialization of the importance of wastewater management, Facilitating partnerships between the government, private sector, and the community in handling domestic wastewater, Strengthening community institutions and optimizing the role of villages in domestic wastewater management, Increasing funding in Domestic Waste Water Management, Increasing hygiene promotions/campaigns/education and sustainable safe sanitation. © Published under an exclusive license by AIP Publishing.

title: Biotower as an Efficient Solution for Food and Beverage Industrial Wastewater Treatment
authors: Shareef N.
abstract: The global food processing industry generates significant volumes of wastewater rich in organic matter, nutrients, oils, and suspended solids. Traditional biological treatments often struggle to meet tightening discharge regulations and circular economy goals focused on resource recovery. As a major contributor to global industrial effluents, the food sector requires effective wastewater treatment to reduce pollution, comply with regulations, and support sustainable water use. Key objectives include minimizing contaminants, conserving water, and recovering valuable byproducts. Among available technologies, Biotower, a biofilm-based aerobic system, offers an energy-efficient and cost-effective solution. Its fixed-media design supports microbial growth for effective pollutant removal. Trickling filters, known for their simplicity and reliability, are also widely used, particularly for variable organic loads. Combining these systems with advanced treatments can enhance performance and support sustainability targets. This chapter highlights innovative and integrated wastewater treatment solutions by Brentwood Industries, tailored for the food industry. It focuses on energy-efficient technologies that optimize treatment performance while minimizing capital and operational costs, particularly for high-strength organic wastewater. Global case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the Biotower system in facilities such as a fish processing plant in Walvis Bay-Namibia, a dairy in Wisconsin U.S, a whisky distillery in Scotland, and a coffee manufacturer in Germany. Notably, the Walvis Bay trickling filter achieved an energy consumption of just 0.11 kWh/m3 (0.16 kWh/kg COD) approximately one-third of that used by conventional activated sludge systems while meeting stringent discharge targets (COD reduced from 1,200 mg/L to 240 mg/L; ammonia from 51 mg/L to 4 mg/L). Trickling filters have been reported to produce 20–40% less sludge reduction compared to activated sludge systems. It concludes a proposed sustainable Biotower configuration designed to manage seasonal fluctuations, high-load food industrial wastewater and support diverse water reuse goals. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Automation of Water Treatment Facilities with Adaptive KPI Integration within a Sustainable Development Strategy
authors: Zaiets N.; Lutska N.; Vlasenko L.; Shtepa V.; Junge S.
abstract: This paper is devoted to the development of engineering methods for integrating a Sustainable Development strategy into automated process control systems of industrial enterprises. The relevance of the study is driven by the need to shift from conventional variables stabilization systems to adaptive control models capable of dynamically responding to environmental and energy-related challenges. An original approach is proposed in which Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) are transformed from reporting tools into dynamic setpoints for local control loops. The authors develop a dynamic model for KPI selection and adjustment based on an integral sustainability compliance index, enabling real-time balancing between environmental requirements – such as wastewater treatment quality indicators – and economic efficiency. The adaptive behavior of the model is achieved through time-dependent weighting coefficients, which are automatically adjusted according to the proximity of monitored process variables to regulatory discharge limits, thereby prioritizing environmental safety under critical operating conditions. Special attention is given to an object-oriented approach that ensures the adaptation of strategic sustainability goals to specific technological units of wastewater treatment facilities. The paper also analyzes the impact of an enterprise’s digital maturity level on the reliability of KPI calculation and proposes the use of soft sensors for forecasting complex environmental variables under conditions of limited instrumentation. The effectiveness of the proposed solutions is validated through simulation modeling of wastewater treatment processes at a dairy processing plant. The results demonstrate that the implementation of the dynamic control model reduces specific energy consumption by 28.1% while fully complying with established environmental regulations. The practical significance of the study lies in the creation of an algorithmic foundation for modernizing industrial process automation systems, enabling the integration of technological reliability with the requirements of the global green transition. © 2026, Anhalt University of Applied Sciences. title: Effect of Water Crisis on Rural Women: A Review of Indian Perspectives
authors: Khatun S.; Aktar N.
abstract: The study examines the profound impact of the water crisis on rural women in India. This paper aims to underscore rural women’s health and educational challenges in India. The study used electronic search engines, such as Google Scholar, PubMed, ResearchGate, Science Direct, and others, with several keywords, to show various aspects of the effects of the water crisis on rural women. The impact of the water crisis on Indian rural women has been evaluated using more than 150 published articles and reports from 2010 to 2024. The investigators then evaluated the full papers and screened them in greater detail against eligibility criteria. The study results illustrated that carrying heavy loads of water contributes to back and neck pain, bone deformities, miscarriages, and pregnancy complications. Water shortages exacerbate these issues, increasing the risk of water-related diseases and malnutrition, particularly among women and infants. The time spent collecting water limits women’s educational opportunities, with many girls missing school due to inadequate sanitation facilities. Additionally, travelling long distances for water exposes women to harassment and violence, leading to stress and poor mental health. The research underscores the urgent need for gender-responsive water policies in India to improve access, strengthen women’s empowerment, and promote gender equality in water management. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Climate Change and Resilience: Need, Challenges and Future
authors: Srivastava R.; Mehara G.; Sharma A.; Gupta M.K.
abstract: Climate change poses a unique global threat, affecting ecosystems, economies, and societies with increasing speed. The increasing frequency of rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and shifting climatic patterns emphasize the need for resilience-building. This chapter describes the concept of resilience in climate change, with a focus on its role in minimizing adverse impacts and ensuring sustainable development. It explores resilience planning challenges, such as financial limitations, policy lacunas, socio-economic inequalities, and technological limitations. It also explores governance, community participation, and scientific invention role in increasing adaptive capacity. The discourse also touches on sector-specific resilience in agriculture, water supply, urban planning, and disaster management, highlighting integrated strategies towards climate adaptation and mitigation. Additionally, the chapter contains best-practice climate resilience programs from around the globe and makes conclusions on how to replicate them. Policymaking for climate resilience is dependent on the future technical developments and the input of businesses, governments, and societies. Climate change needs to be addressed through a shift in paradigms toward sustainable development, equitable resource sharing, and robust institutional arrangements. The chapter ends by highlighting the imperative of a whole-of-society, cross-disciplinary approach to climate resilience aligned with universal sustainability objectives. With increasing intensity of climate problems, building resilience is no longer a choice but an imperative for ensuring a habitable future for everyone. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: 'Ooru Alert'- A Crowdsourced Urban Issue Reporting System for Bengaluru
authors: Anandhi R.J.; Sasikala T.; Pillai D.R.; Gadi P.; Aradya S.V.; Prasathkannan A.
abstract: In order to solve municipal concerns in Bengaluru, this research investigates the development and impact of a crowdsourcing application for reporting urban issues. Residents may use the app to instantly report a variety of urban issues, such as poor infrastructure, traffic jams, water supply issues, and road upkeep. To enable targeted responses, these submissions are sent to the relevant civic authorities, including the Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC), Bengaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB), Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP), and BESCOM. The application contributes to the overall improvement of urban government and public service delivery in Bengaluru by fostering better communication between residents and municipal entities, increasing the effectiveness of problem resolution, and promoting accountability and transparency. The application's capacity to promote civic engagement and cooperative approach to urban administration is also evaluated in the report. © 2026 IEEE.

title: SMART SUSTAINABLE CITIES AND COMMUNITIES FOR PEOPLE: A PATHWAY TO A RESILIENT FUTURE
authors: Irfanullah Arfeen M.; Sarantis D.; Mujtaba A.; Danish M.; Naseeb J.; Brohi P.; ul Ain N.
abstract: Rapid urbanization in the 21st century demands innovative solutions to address social equity, environmental sustainability, and efficient resource management. Smart Sustainable Cities and Communities (SSCCs) have emerged as a promising paradigm integrating advanced technologies, data-driven governance, and citizen engagement to create inclusive, resilient, and livable urban environments. This study examines the role of technology in facilitating the transition toward SSCCs and its contribution to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Using an extensive literature review and quantitative research, this paper identifies technological enablers-such as artificial intelligence (AI), big data, and the Internet of Things (IoT)-as catalysts for improving resource efficiency, waste management, environmental protection, and service delivery. Particular attention is given to SDGs related to good health and well-being, quality education, decent work and economic growth, climate action, and affordable clean energy. The findings indicate that technology significantly contributes to smart city development and supports SDG achievement. Future research should examine stakeholder roles-including government, industry, academia, and policy institutions-and explore additional SDGs such as poverty reduction, gender equality, and clean water and sanitation. The study concludes that technology plays a transformative role in advancing sustainable development through smart sustainable cities. © ISES 2026.

title: Municipalities as spaces for social innovation: A public relations and participation perspective
authors: Motloutsi E.
abstract: The South African local government is the closest to the people and provides public services such as sanitation, burial grounds, electricity, water, and other essential services, working in partnership with provincial and national government (Oelofse, 2010). All three areas of government cooperate through a system called cooperative management, which facilitates a collective approach to service delivery and resource sharing. However, there are concerns about the slow pace of development and innovation in local governments in meeting citizens’ demands and responding to the 21st-Century Development Agenda. This chapter explores municipalities as innovative spaces for facilitating development and for responding to the degradation of local governance through public participation as a strategic communication process. Social innovation and public participation are more than governance systems; rather, they are communicative processes that require an effective communication strategy to function effectively and achieve their strategic goals. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Corné Meintjes, Dalien Rene Benecke and Padhma Samantha Moodley; individual chapters, the contributors

title: Community empowerment in tuberculosis elimination
authors: Arora V.K.; Rajpal S.; Anand A.
abstract: In public health, meaningful community engagement has consistently been linked to improved access to timely diagnosis, strengthened treatment adherence, reduced stigma, and better overall health outcomes, particularly among marginalized and underserved populations. Effective engagement fosters trust, enhances service utilization, and promotes sustained care-seeking behaviour. However, genuine empowerment extends beyond simple participation in health programs; it encompasses the ability of communities to influence local governance processes and address broader social determinants such as nutrition, sanitation, education, and livelihood security, while functioning as a dynamic and transformative process that shifts communities from passive beneficiaries to active agents of health action.Community empowerment operates through interconnected logistical and psychological pathways. Logistical support improves access to diagnosis, treatment continuation, and linkage with health systems, while psychosocial reinforcement through peer support and survivor engagement strengthens motivation, reduces internalized stigma, and sustains long-term adherence. At the same time, empowerment is shaped by local socio-economic realities, including poverty and livelihood insecurity, and may face risks such as volunteer burnout, stigma toward community workers, inequitable reliance on unpaid labor, and limited financial sustainability—underscoring the need for ethical safeguards and social protection.Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health challenge despite the availability of effective chemotherapy. According to the World Health Organization, TB continues to affect millions annually and remains a leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide. Within the End TB Strategy, community engagement and civil-society participation—including contributions from national and nongovernmental organizations—are recognized as critical to sustainable TB control.TB elimination therefore requires not only biomedical interventions but also ethically supported, economically feasible, and institutionally sustained community empowerment capable of transforming participation into shared ownership of tuberculosis control. © 2026 Tuberculosis Association of India. title: Sustainable Water Management: Strategies for Addressing Global Water Scarcity
authors: Alshammari S.F.; Al Mubarak M.
abstract: Water scarcity is an escalating global crisis that affects billions of people, with profound implications for public health, ecosystems, and economic development. This problem is due to climate change, population growth, urbanization, and poor water management. Solving this challenge requires knowledge of its causes and ways of using water resources effectively and sustainably. Therefore, this study aims to identify measures for efficient water management at the technology, policy, and community levels. These approaches are meant to reduce the effects of water shortage and increase access to fresh water. The study includes a systematic literature review, case studies, and a conceptual model based on technology, policy, and community-based interventions. The study calls for enhanced Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM), state-of-the-art water recycling, active community involvement, and effective adaptive governance to combat water scarcity conditions. However, the study also reveals challenges such as political will, lack of funds, and inadequate water governance. This research provides novel findings in sustainable water management by integrating theory and practice. The paper offers valuable suggestions for policymakers, water institutions, and local governments and stresses the multi-level and multi-agent governance approach. The results are timely as they are under the backdrop of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and, more specifically, the goal of clean water and sanitation (SDG 6). In filling the knowledge gap on sustainable practices, this study presents a framework for future research and practice addressing global water scarcity. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Real-Time AI-Powered Monitoring and Automation System for Industrial Graywater Recycling
authors: Padmapriya T.M.; Thamaraiselvi V.; Ramya R.; Porkodi V.; Ranjitha P.
abstract: The friendly green intelligent system helps in real-time surveillance of industrial graywater and subsequently provides effective recycle. The solution uses AI with Internet of Things (IoT) sensors to increase efficiency in water treatment and to comply with water environmental regulations. The major objective of the system is the reduction of wastewater through an intelligent decision making and automation. The proposed solution features a multi-step filtration and monitoring setup. It begins with a biological oxygen demand (BOD) sensor to detect levels of organic contamination. If the values exceed safe limits identified using mathematical threshold models, the system automatically shuts off motors and sends alerts to prevent further processing of polluted water. Initial physical filtration is carried out using a dirt filter followed by a migration filter. Chemical characteristics are then analyzed using a pH sensor, while turbidity sensors evaluate water clarity. To further ensure safety, MQ-3 sensors monitor harmful gases, and UV sterilization is used to eliminate pathogens. All stages are managed through real-time feedback and conditional automation logic, accessible via a mobile app. During testing, the system showed fast and accurate responses to water quality changes. The system's intelligent feature helps to detect unusual sensor readings early and allows quick action like shutting down operations and alerting the maintenance team. The collected sensor data support predictive maintenance, which avoid breakdowns and improve system reliability. This smart setup makes graywater recycling most effective, with over 70% of water being reused in industry by combining real-time monitoring with automated controls. © 2026 Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Genthiner Straße 13, 10785 Berlin, Germany.

title: Deciphering the Water Accessibility in Urban Neighbourhoods: A Case of Water Supply in Delhi
authors: Kumar S.; Mishra S.; Kumar A.
abstract: The growing population brings along an increased demand for infrastructure and services in our cities; hence, city managers will never stop working to meet that demand. Water shortage is one of the main bottlenecks to urbanization, together with other fundamental societal needs. The Urban Local Body (ULB) or Municipal Corporation in an urban region takes responsibility to provide safe drinking water and availability of water supply for all domestic, commercial, and industrial purposes, as per the 12th Schedule of the Indian Constitution. According to Sustainable Development Goals, 2030, especially SDG-6, all sections of society should have access to and management of water and sanitation services. This research will evaluate the water accessibility in urban neighbourhoods of Delhi and will also assess the role of Urban Local Body and other agencies in it. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: From Expansion to Exclusion: Urbanization, Spatial Inequality, and Child Streetism in Nigeria
authors: Jelili M.O.; Oyewole K.A.; Simon F.R.
abstract: This chapter systematically reviews the intersection of urbanization, spatial inequality, and the street child phenomenon in Nigeria between 2015 and 2025. Nigeria's rapid urban growth, while transformative, has deepened inequality and exacerbated child vulnerability, particularly in informal settlements where housing, sanitation, and basic services are inadequate. The review synthesizes evidence from 64 academic and policy sources, highlighting structural drivers such as unregulated urban expansion, poverty, educational exclusion, and weak governance frameworks. Findings reveal that children in marginalized urban spaces face multidimensional risks including malnutrition, exploitation, and intergenerational cycles of deprivation. Despite existing policies, interventions remain fragmented, poorly enforced, and rarely child-sensitive. Comparative lessons from other contexts demonstrate that integrated, participatory, and child-focused governance can reduce vulnerability. The chapter concludes by calling for systemic reforms that embed child protection in urban development, prioritize spatial equity, and strengthen institutional capacity to disrupt pathways that push children into street survival. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, David V. Ogunkan; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: Indigenous Water Infrastructure: Lessons from Alaska Native Communities
authors: Nartey M.; Poleacovschi C.; Hill C.G.
abstract: Many Alaska Native (AN) communities face significant water insecurity challenges, including limited access to piped water, outdated and aging water infrastructure, and poor sanitation services. Conducting water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) research and engineering projects in AN communities requires a deep understanding of the AN cultural context. These communities possess unique values, governance systems, and traditional knowledge integral to their identity and way of life. This chapter explores the state of WASH-related research and engineering in AN communities, focusing on the importance of culturally sensitive approaches emphasizing community-based participatory research (CBPR). Using a case study format based on the authors’ experiences with water insecurity research in Unalakleet, Alaska, this chapter illustrates how a CBPR-based framework can be effectively applied. The authors highlight the collaborative process of gaining community approval, navigating complex approval procedures, and building lasting partnerships that prioritize community engagement. This chapter also offers practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners in the WASH sector, detailing how to work more effectively with indigenous communities, navigate complex approval processes, and integrate CBPR principles to ensure sustainable, community-driven outcomes while acknowledging that every community has unique needs and expectations. © 2026 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. title: Gendered Dimensions of Water Security and Food Supply: Examining Women’s Health and Leadership in Gangani Census Mouza, West Bengal
authors: Sarkar A.; Basak S.; Jana S.; Halder O.; Bhowal A.
abstract: The gender aspect is essential when it comes to access to water and food. The study is concentrated on the Gangani village of Garhbeta. A significant part of the village is dominated by rapid gully erosion and the formation of Badlands. A substantial part of the village is covered by agricultural land and forest. Households are located in the northeastern and southwestern parts of the village, surrounded by badland topography. The people of Gangani mouza are living in the Badlands. As per the 2011 census, the village had 500 households. Now it has approximately increased to 650. One hundred household surveys were conducted to carry out the present study. Household surveys were conducted using seven sets of questionnaires and interviews with village women. A random stratified sampling method has been employed. The objectives of the study are to identify how women obtain, manage, and use water for household purposes. It is also aimed at determining the impact of water insecurity on women’s physical and mental health, including issues related to sanitation and proper nutrition. Another aim is to evaluate women’s participation in community water governance and decision-making. A frequency distribution table has been prepared based on the survey data. Different chart methods through MS Excel have been employed for the graphical representation of data. The comprehensive relationship between gender roles, access to natural resources, and social well-being has been adequately identified. The women in Gangani village play a significant role in resource management and community leadership. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.
